kept.title: Rail mode tabs and the Style, Lighting and Tools radio groups ignore arrow keys
kept.evidence: kb.cjs 1: ArrowRight on the focused Surfaces tab leaves focus and selection unchanged, and all 5 tabs are separate Tab stops with no aria-controls or tabpanel. The panel is a <section aria-label>. radio.cjs: in the 'Design style' radiogroup, ArrowRight and ArrowDown do nothing. The editor's global ←/→ handler deliberately skips [role=tablist] and [role=radiogroup], so arrows are dead there. The changes dot is an aria-label on a bare span, read as 'has changes Surfaces' (radio.cjs tabs aria).
kept.repro: Tab to the Surfaces tab and press ArrowRight. Open Style, focus 'None' and press ArrowRight.
kept.fix: ModeTabs: roving tabindex (selected tab 0, others -1), Arrow, Home and End move and select, id and aria-controls to a role=tabpanel wrapper in panelWrap. Style, lighting and tools cards: roving tabindex plus arrows, or build them on the house Chips radio-group logic. Replace the dot's aria-label with visually hidden text after the label (', has changes').

verdict.reason: The code matches the finding, so I didn't need to run it on :3020. In rail.tsx, ModeTabs renders role="tablist" with five role="tab" buttons. There is no onKeyDown, no tabIndex handling (so every tab is its own Tab stop), and no id, aria-controls or tabpanel; the panel is a `<section aria-label>`. The changes dot is `<span aria-label="has changes">` on a bare span, which screen readers handle unreliably. style-panel.tsx:44 and lighting-panel.tsx:34 are role="radiogroup" groups of role="radio" buttons with no key handling. In visualizer-editor.tsx:517 the global ←/→ handler returns early when focus is inside [role=tablist] or [role=radiogroup], so arrow keys do nothing in those controls. Two corrections to the suggested fix. First, the house Chips (components/om/chips.tsx) has no arrow-key logic either, so building the cards on Chips would not add arrows. Second, the house Tabs (components/om/tabs.tsx:27-41) already has roving tabindex with Arrow, Home and End; that is the pattern to mirror. Severity minor is right: the mouse and Tab paths work, but it is a WAI-ARIA pattern violation on the editor's main navigation.
verdict.fix:
1) Add a small pure house helper, components/om/roving.ts. It exports `rovingKey(e, selector)`: it handles ArrowLeft/Right/Up/Down, Home and End, moves focus among the matching elements (wrapping at the ends) and returns the next element, the same logic as the onKeyDown in components/om/tabs.tsx. Reuse it in om/tabs.tsx so there is one implementation.
2) ModeTabs (components/visualizer/editor/rail.tsx):
   - Roving tabindex: 0 on the selected tab, -1 on the others.
   - onKeyDown on the tablist calls rovingKey, then onMode() on the new tab. Selection follows focus, which is fine because switching panels is instant client state.
   - Give each tab id=`viz-tab-${key}` and aria-controls=`viz-panel`.
   - Wrap the active panel in panelWrap as a role="tabpanel" with id="viz-panel", aria-labelledby set to the active tab's id and tabIndex={0}. Keep the inner Panel section's label.
   - Replace the dot's aria-label with aria-hidden on the dot, plus a visually hidden ", has changes" span after the label text. Use the repo's existing sr-only class if there is one, otherwise a tiny rail.module.css rule.
   - The ≤1024 dock variant gets the same code for free.
3) Style and Lighting cards (style-panel.tsx, lighting-panel.tsx):
   - Roving tabindex: 0 on the checked radio, or on the first one when none is checked; -1 on the rest.
   - onKeyDown on the radiogroup calls rovingKey and then picks the focused option, as the APG radio pattern does.
   - Style: arrow keys must select, not toggle; the click's toggle-off behaviour stays.
4) Tools: its radiogroup is ChoiceCard-based. Apply the same roving tabindex and arrow-key selection there, and to ChoiceCard/Chips generally if the owner wants it app-wide; that is a separate, larger REG.
5) Log as a REG bug fix and add a keyboard check to the visualizer probe: ArrowRight on the Surfaces tab moves focus to and selects Furniture, and ArrowRight in Design style checks the next card.

kept.title: Markers have no visible focus ring, and their names don't say what they are or what finish they carry
kept.evidence: motion-a11y/marker-focus.png: the focused marker looks the same as the others. stage.module.css sets `.dot:focus-visible { outline: none }` and only grows 16→22px, while tab.cjs shows markers at 16x16 with outline none. The aria snapshot lists loose buttons 'White Painted Back Wall', 'Light Oak Floor'…: the photo's original description even after sage paint, with no kind (surface or piece), no current or pending finish, and no group. The furniture markers' action icons (remove, replace, customize) aren't announced.
kept.repro: Tab past 'Got it' into the photo and try to see which square has focus. Read the markers with a screen reader.
kept.fix: .dot:focus-visible { box-shadow: 0 0 0 2px var(--om-color-surface-default), 0 0 0 4px var(--om-color-primary-default), var(--om-elevation-level-3); }. aria-label = `${group word} · ${finish now}${pending ? ` → ${pending}` : ''}` for surfaces, and `${piece} · ${action}` for furniture. Wrap the markers in <div role="group" aria-label="Surfaces on the photo"> (or 'Furniture on the photo').

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this from the code, so I didn't run a live check.

**Focus ring.** `stage.module.css:22` sets `.dot:hover, .dot:focus-visible { width: 22px; height: 22px; outline: none; }`. That is the only focus treatment the markers get. Markers already at 22px show nothing extra on focus: action markers (`remove`, `replace` and `customize`, lines 25–27) are 22px, and targets and selected markers are 24px. So a focused action or selected marker looks exactly like its neighbours. An unselected surface marker only grows from 16 to 22px, and a mouse hover does the same, so focus can't be told apart. The house primitives mark focus with `outline: var(--om-border-2) solid var(--om-color-primary-default); outline-offset: 2px` (the pin, the handle, the link and the card in `components/om/*`).

**Names.** `stage.tsx:130` sets `aria-label={titleCaseLabel(m.label)}`. In `visualizer-editor.tsx:186-191`, `m.label` is the photo reading's raw `s.label` / `f.label`, so it keeps the original description after a new finish is picked. The new finish reaches the dot only as the `--fill` colour. The furniture action shows only as an unlabelled icon (`close`, `palette`, `swap_horiz`), and nothing is announced for it. `aria-pressed` does announce selection. The markers have no group wrapper.

**Severity.** Minor fits: the markers still work by keyboard, but they can't be seen when focused and their names are misleading.
verdict.fix:
1. **Focus ring (`stage.module.css`).** Use the house focus ring instead of a custom box-shadow. Split line 22:
   - `.dot:hover { width: 22px; height: 22px; }`
   - `.dot:focus-visible { outline: var(--om-border-2) solid var(--om-color-primary-default); outline-offset: 2px; }`

   Keep the size growth for hover only. The outline then shows on action, selected and target markers too, and the round furniture dots get a round ring from `border-radius`.

2. **Richer names (`visualizer-editor.tsx:186-191`).** Add an optional `name: string` to the `Marker` type in `stage.tsx`.
   - For surfaces, build it as `${groupWord(s.label)} · ${pendingMaterialName ?? 'as photographed'}`. Take the finish name from the same `resolve(mid)?.name` the change chips use at line 278, so the words match the chips (`Wall → Sage`).
   - For furniture, build it as `${titleCaseLabel(normFurnitureKey(f.label))}${p && p.action !== 'keep' ? ` · ${Remove|Replace|Customize}` : ''}`, which matches the chip wording at line 285.

   Pass `aria-label={target ? \`Take ${name} off the list\` : name}` in `stage.tsx:130`, and keep `aria-pressed`. Leave the visible Tooltip as it is, or feed it the same string. Don't invent a new "current finish" word; reuse the chips' vocabulary.

3. **Group (`stage.tsx`).** Wrap the mapped markers in `<div role="group" aria-label={mode === 'surfaces' ? 'Surfaces on the photo' : 'Furniture on the photo'}>`. Style the wrapper with `display: contents` so the positioning is untouched, and pass the label down from the editor.

   The group label is invented copy, so log it in `REGISTER.md` as an a11y bug fix.

4. **Check.** Tab past "Got it", screenshot a focused action marker and a focused selected marker at 1440, and read the aria snapshot.

kept.title: The versions strip hides its badges and descriptors from assistive tech, and version changes aren't announced
kept.evidence: aria.cjs snapshot: the strip is an unnamed 'list', because aria-label="Versions" sits on a plain div and is ignored. Tiles read 'Show V2' with content '1 2'. The descriptor ('Walls, Floor +1') and the client's favourite, 1 note, 2 pins and 'shared' badges are tooltip-only spans inside a button whose aria-label overrides them. kb.cjs 2c: after ←/→ changes the version, every live region is empty, so nothing tells a screen reader which render is now on the canvas.
kept.repro: Take an accessibility snapshot of the strip, then press ArrowLeft on the page body.
kept.fix: Put aria-label='Versions' on the role=list (or make the strip a region). Tile aria-label = `Show V2 · Walls, Floor +1${fav ? ' · the client’s favourite' : ''}${notes ? ` · ${notes} notes` : ''}${pins ? ` · ${pins} pins` : ''}${shared ? ' · shared' : ''}`. Add a visually hidden aria-live='polite' span in the editor fed by setView ('V2 · Walls, Floor +1 on screen').

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this by reading the code. I did not run anything live, because the code settles it.
1. In versions-strip.tsx (line 58), aria-label="Versions" sits on a plain <div> with no role. A generic element can't carry a name, so screen readers ignore it, and the role="list" on line 60 is left unnamed.
2. Each tile's button has an aria-label, "Show V2" or "V2 (on screen)". That label replaces the button's contents as its accessible name. So the favourite, notes, pins and shared badges, which are tooltip-wrapped spans inside the button (lines 36-43), never reach assistive tech.
3. One detail is off in the finding. The descriptor ("V2 · Walls, Floor +1") is not inside the button. It is a visible sibling span on line 45, so browse mode can read it. It is still missing from the button's name, which is what someone tabbing or using the arrow keys hears.
4. The only live regions in components/visualizer are the topbar's Saving/Saved text and the stage's "running" status. setView (visualizer-editor.tsx:112, called from the ←/→ handler on line 520 and from onPick on line 609) announces nothing. The stage image does swap its alt, but a changed alt is not announced.

The severity of minor stands. A studio using a screen reader would feel it, but most demo viewers would not.
verdict.fix:
1. versions-strip.tsx: remove aria-label from the outer div and make the strip a labelled list. Give the head title an id and put aria-labelledby={id} (or aria-label="Versions") on the role="list" div.
2. versions-strip.tsx: build the button's aria-label from the version's details: `${on ? label + ' (on screen)' : 'Show ' + label}${sub ? ' · ' + sub : ''}`. Then append the badges, reusing the tooltip wording that already exists: ' · the client’s favourite', ' · N notes from the client', ' · N pins', ' · shared with the client'. Mark the badges span aria-hidden so nothing is read twice.
3. visualizer-editor.tsx: add one <span className="visually-hidden" aria-live="polite"> (the global class in app/globals.css:128, already used by applied-dot.tsx). Feed it the view key's label and descriptor, e.g. "V2 · Walls, Floor +1 on screen" or "Original photo on screen". Derive the text in render from the current view key, not from an effect that sets state, so it follows the ESLint rule against setState in effects.
No visual change, so no REGISTER entry is needed beyond a one-line bug fix note.

kept.title: Reduced motion isn't honoured by the motion-driven transitions, and durations are hard-coded
kept.where: Editor stage crossfade, banner, running card, all widths
kept.evidence: rm.cjs with reducedMotion 'reduce': 60ms after ArrowLeft both stage images are still mid-fade (opacities 0.63 and 0.37), so the full 280ms crossfade runs. No <MotionConfig reducedMotion="user"> exists anywhere (grep), although globals.css:280-281 says motion surfaces need it. The durations are literals: stage.tsx photo 0.28, banner 0.15, running 0.2; pin-card.module.css 160ms; editor.module.css tray 200ms; stage.module.css barFill 300ms. They don't come from lib/motion (duration.sheet, toggle, modal).
kept.repro: Emulate prefers-reduced-motion: reduce and switch versions with ←.
kept.fix: Wrap the (editor), renders and AppShell layouts in <MotionConfig reducedMotion="user">, as the globals.css contract asks. Replace the literals with lib/motion tokens (duration.sheet with ease.standard for the crossfade, duration.toggle for the banner, overlayFade for the running card) and CSS vars (--motion-toggle, --motion-modal).

verdict.reason:
The observation holds. No MotionConfig exists anywhere in app/, components/ or lib/; the only hit is the comment at globals.css:281 asking for one. The only reduced-motion-aware motion component is components/quotes/editor/section-card.tsx, which calls useReducedMotion. stage.tsx hard-codes its transitions: banner 0.15 (line 99), the photo crossfade 0.28 (line 116) and the running card 0.2 (line 149). None of them read lib/motion.

Three parts of the finding are off:
1. **The proposed fix would not fix the reported symptom.** With motion's `<MotionConfig reducedMotion="user">`, only transform and layout animations are skipped; opacity still animates. The crossfade is opacity-only, so it would keep running the full 280ms. The wrapper only helps the banner's y slide.
2. **The CSS literals already honour reduced motion.** pin-card.module.css:23 and editor.module.css:43 turn their keyframes off (`animation: none`) under prefers-reduced-motion. The barFill transition is cut to 80ms by the global rule in globals.css:282-287. For CSS, the problem is only token hygiene, not an a11y bug.
3. **The gap is app-wide, not specific to the visualizer.** Putting per-layout wrappers in (editor) and renders would leave every other motion surface uncovered.

A soft 280ms opacity fade under reduced motion is low harm; this is a polish or minor issue, not a visible break.

kept.title: Phone tray: the layout snaps around a 24px slide, and closing is an instant cut
kept.evidence: motion-a11y/tray-60.png: 60ms after tapping Lighting, the rooms row and strip are already gone and the photo has jumped from 326px to 218px wide, while only the tray fades up 24px. tray-close-30.png: 30ms after the second tap the tray is gone and the rooms row, strip and full-size photo are back, with no exit motion. The tray is conditionally rendered with a CSS keyframe only (editor.module.css .tray trayUp).
kept.repro: 390x844 touch editor: tap Lighting in the dock, then tap it again.
kept.fix: Wrap the tray in AnimatePresence with lib/motion sheetRise (enter duration.sheet, exit sheetExit). Keep the strip mounted and let the tray overlay it like a sheet, or animate the stage's height, so the photo doesn't jump. Move focus into the tray's panel head on open and back to the dock tab on close.

verdict.reason: The code confirms it. In visualizer-editor.tsx (lines 634–645), the narrow editor does three things when the tray opens. It unmounts the rooms row (`rooms.length && !tray`) and the strip (`{!tray ? strip : null}`), and mounts the tray conditionally (`tray && panel ? <div className={styles.tray}>`). The only motion is the CSS keyframe `trayUp` in editor.module.css:35–36, a 24px slide with a fade on enter. So the rooms row and strip disappear in one frame and the flex `.body` stage shrinks at once, which is why the photo jumps from about 326 to 218px wide. Closing unmounts the tray with no exit, and the rooms row and strip come back instantly. The auditor's tray-60.png shows this state: at 60ms the tray is up and the rooms row and strip are gone. There is no AnimatePresence, and no focus handling on open or close. lib/motion.ts already has `sheetRise` (exit uses `duration.sheetExit`) and `duration.sheet`, so the house token exists but isn't used here. Severity stays minor: the tray works, but opening it on a phone throws the layout around with no motion to connect the two states, a jolt a studio would notice in a live demo.
verdict.fix:
In components/visualizer/editor/visualizer-editor.tsx:
1. Wrap the tray in `<AnimatePresence initial={false}>` and render it as `<motion.div key="tray" className={styles.tray} variants={sheetRise} initial="initial" animate="animate" exit="exit">` from lib/motion. Its enter uses `duration.sheet`, its exit `duration.sheetExit`, and it follows `useReducedMotion`, the same as the house's other sheets.
2. Wrap the rooms row and the strip in AnimatePresence too, as `motion.div`s that collapse `height: 'auto' → 0` and fade on `duration.sheetExit`. Put `layout` on the stage wrapper (`.body`), so the photo scales between the two sizes on the same curve instead of snapping.
3. Remove the `trayUp` keyframe and its reduced-motion override from editor.module.css:35–36 and :43, since the motion variants now handle both.
4. Focus: when the tray opens, send focus to the panel's heading or first control. When it closes (a second tap, `PanelClose`, or the room chip), return focus to the active dock tab via a ref on ModeTabs' dock button. This is a small effect keyed on `tray` that reads refs in the effect, not during render.
Verify at 390×844 touch with frame shots at 0, 60 and 200ms on open and on close, plus a reduced-motion pass.

kept.title: Phone: the Maison AI button covers the versions strip
kept.evidence: motion-a11y/final-m-editor.png and m-pin-mode.png: the FAB (x≈326-374, y≈656-704) sits on top of V2's tile, hiding its note, pin and shared badges and its kebab. editor.module.css `.editor[data-narrow] .fab { bottom: calc(60px + 68px + 12px …) }` clears the dock and go bar but not the ~100px strip.
kept.repro: Open the editor at 390x844 and look at the strip's right end.
kept.fix: Add the strip's height to the narrow FAB offset (or measure it through a CSS var set on the strip), or hide the FAB at ≤767 in the editor as the tray state already does, keeping Maison AI in the design's ⋯ menu.

verdict.reason: The overlap is real. In final-m-editor.png at 390×844 the Maison AI FAB sits on V2's tile and hides its badges and kebab. The editor already means to leave room for the FAB at the end of the strip. It sets `--viz-strip-end` (96px, and 72px under `data-narrow`), and `.strip` in versions-strip.module.css uses that variable as its right padding, so the tile scroller (`.row`) stops short of the FAB. The narrow FAB offset (bottom 140px, right 16px, so y≈656–704 and x≈326–374) also puts the FAB inside the strip's band (y≈628–730), as intended. What breaks it is the `@media (max-width: 1024px)` rule in versions-strip.module.css: it rewrites the strip's padding to `var(--om-spacing-2) var(--om-spacing-3)` on all four sides. That drops the 72px end space, so the scroller runs under the FAB. The bug therefore hits every width at or below 1024 (phones and tablets), and while the tray is open it does not show, because the FAB is hidden then. Raising the FAB above the strip, as the auditor suggests, would put it over the canvas toolbar or the photo. Hiding the FAB would drop a shell piece the house rules require (REG-507). The real bug is the lost padding.
verdict.fix: In components/visualizer/editor/versions-strip.module.css, keep the reserved end in the ≤1024 rule. Change `.strip { padding: var(--om-spacing-2) var(--om-spacing-3); … }` to `.strip { padding: var(--om-spacing-2) var(--viz-strip-end, var(--om-spacing-3)) var(--om-spacing-2) var(--om-spacing-3); … }`. `data-narrow` already sets `--viz-strip-end` to 72px, which covers the 48px FAB at right:16 plus 8px of air. The tile scroller then ends before the FAB and the last tile's badges and kebab scroll into view. editor.module.css needs no change. Check at 390×844 touch and 768×1024 that the FAB's box does not intersect `.row`'s rect, and that 1440 is unchanged.

kept.title: The go bar says '1 change waiting' while the button says 'Generate · 2 changes'
kept.evidence: motion-a11y/tray-open.png and tray-close-30.png: the same footer reads '1 change waiting' beside 'Generate · 2 changes'. The text counts the grouped change chips (visualizer-editor.tsx `changes`), but the button's intent label counts surfaces.
kept.repro: Pick one finish for Walls (2 surfaces) and look at the compact footer at 390.
kept.fix: Count one unit in both places: build intent.label from changes.length, or word the compact text from the intent count.

verdict.reason: The two counts come from different sources, and the screenshot shows the mismatch. `intentFor` (lib/visualizer/model.ts:150-160) counts each surface on its own, so `materials` is the number of surface ids and the label reads `Generate · ${changes} changes`. The editor's `changes` list (visualizer-editor.tsx:272-293) instead groups surfaces by groupWord plus finish, and furniture by kind plus action. So one finish on Walls (2 surfaces) is 1 chip but 2 intent changes. The compact footer (rail.tsx:76) prints "1 change waiting" from `changes.length` beside the button's "Generate · 2 changes". motion-a11y/tray-open.png at 390 shows exactly that. The same mismatch appears on desktop, where the head reads "Your changes · 1" (rail.tsx:84) above the same "Generate · 2 changes" button. So it is not only a compact-footer problem. It is a minor copy issue: the numbers disagree, but nothing breaks.

In the edit branch, label with `const n = o.shown ?? changes` and `n > 1 ? `Generate · ${n} changes` : 'Generate'`. In visualizer-editor.tsx, build the `changes: Change[]` list before calling `intentFor`: move the block at 272-293 above line 121, or compute `intent` after it. Then pass `shown: changes.length`. Keep the raw per-surface count in `Intent.changes` in case anything else reads it, and grep for other readers of `intent.changes` first. This makes the button, the compact "n changes waiting" and the desktop "Your changes · n" agree at every width. No new UI.

kept.title: Present: the image hard-cuts, thumbnails show no state, and the active thumbnail can be off screen
kept.evidence: motion-a11y/present.png: the thumbnail row scrolls sideways inside the 280px side column, so V2 is half-cut and V3 is hidden with no cue. The aria snapshot shows thumbnail buttons 'Original', 'V1'… with no pressed or current state, and .thumb has no focus-visible rule. ← and → swap with a hard cut, while the canvas crossfades the same change.
kept.repro: Open Present from the canvas bar and press ← or →.
kept.fix: Wrap the picture's image in AnimatePresence with the stage's crossfade tokens. Add aria-current='true' on the active thumbnail and a focus-visible ring, and scrollIntoView({inline:'nearest'}) on key change. Let the thumbnails wrap in a grid in the side column rather than a hidden horizontal scroll.

verdict.reason: Mostly confirmed from the code in present-dialog.tsx, with one part wrong. What holds: - **Hard cut.** The stage renders a plain ``, so ← / → and the thumbnails swap the picture with a hard cut. The canvas does the same change with a crossfade: stage.tsx wraps `motion.img key={image}` in `AnimatePresence initial={false}` with opacity 0→1 over 0.28s. - **No active state.** The thumbnails only get `data-on`, which is purely visual. They have no `aria-current` or `aria-pressed`, so a screen reader cannot tell which version is showing. - **Hidden thumbnails.** `.thumbs` is `display:flex; overflow-x:auto` inside the 280px `.side` column. Each `.thumb` is `flex: 0 0 104px` with an 8px gap, so only about 2.5 fit. With Original + V1…V3, the later versions sit off to the right with no cue. Nothing scrolls the active thumbnail into view when ← / → moves past the visible ones. What is wrong: - **Focus ring.** The claim that `.thumb` has no focus-visible rule is misleading. app/globals.css:123 sets a global `:focus-visible { outline: var(--om-border-2) solid var(--om-color-primary-default); outline-offset: 2px }`, and `.thumb` does not suppress it. Keyboard focus already shows the house ring, so that part of the fix is not needed. I did not run it live; the code paths are unambiguous. Severity stays polish.
verdict.fix: present-dialog.tsx: - Crossfade the picture like the canvas does. Import `AnimatePresence, motion` from 'motion/react' and replace the bare `` with ``. Use the same values as stage.tsx, or the `lib/motion` token if one matches. - Add `aria-current={x.key === key ? 'true' : undefined}` on each thumbnail button. - Keep the active thumbnail in view: give the thumbs container a ref, and in an effect on `[key, open]` run `querySelector('[data-on]')?.scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest', inline: 'nearest' })`. Running it in an effect is fine, since it sets no state. dialogs.module.css: - Let the exiting and entering images overlap by stacking them in one grid cell. Make `.presentStage` `display: grid; place-items: center` and give `.presentStage > img` `grid-area: 1 / 1`. The absolutely positioned nav buttons are unaffected. - Replace the hidden sideways scroll with a wrapping grid inside the already vertically scrolling `.side`: `.thumbs { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr)); gap: var(--om-spacing-2); }`, `.thumb { flex: none; }`, `.thumb img { width: 100%; height: auto; aspect-ratio: 104 / 66; }`. - In the ≤1024 media block, where `.side` drops under the picture at 180px tall, use `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(104px, 1fr))` instead. No new focus rule is needed; the global `:focus-visible` ring already applies. This is a bug fix, so log it in REGISTER.md as source `bug fix`.

kept.title: The highlight overlay and lighting preview pop in with no fade, and flicker between selections
kept.evidence: stage.tsx renders viz-highlight and viz-preview as plain with no transition. In visualizer-editor.tsx `highlight = hl && hl.key === hlKey ? hl.url : null`, so the old overlay disappears the moment the selection changes and the new one arrives after the 40ms timer plus regionOverlay, giving a blank frame between surfaces. The breathe animation itself works (gen2.cjs opacity samples 0.55→0.89→0.59).
kept.repro: Click the Walls marker, then the Floor marker, and watch the lit region.
kept.fix: Keep the last overlay until the next one resolves (store the previous url), and fade overlay changes in and out with AnimatePresence at duration.toggle. Do the same for the lighting preview.

verdict.reason: The finding is real, and the lighting half is worse than reported. Both overlays are keyed so they drop out as soon as their key changes. `highlight = hl && hl.key === hlKey ? hl.url : null` (visualizer-editor.tsx:214) and `pv && pv.key === pvKey ? pv.url : null` (line 229) both return null until the async result for the new key arrives. In stage.tsx:121/123 both are plain conditional elements with no enter or exit motion. The only animation is the `breathe` keyframe on .highlight, which starts straight at opacity 0.9. Live check on :3018 (Kevin Ng's design, 1440): I selected 'White Painted Back Wall', then clicked 'Light Oak Floor' and sampled each frame with rAF. For about 80 ms (4 frames) there was no viz-highlight at all, then the new overlay appeared at full strength. So the region blinks off and pops back on. The lighting preview has the same logic, but its debounce is 90 ms and every knob change resets that timer. The upload path (`visualizer-editor.tsx` lines 349 and 367) calls `fallbackDetection(fallbackDots(img))`. `model.ts` line 53 clips Walls to `within: [0,0.04,1,0.8]`, line 54 clips Floor to `[0,0.5,1,1]` and line 56 clips Ceiling to `[0,0,1,0.3]`. `segment.ts` turns those boxes into hard `blocked` pixels, which causes all three artefacts:

- the straight seam at y=0.50 where Floor stops,
- the straight line at y=0.30 where Ceiling stops.

The seeds come from `fallback.ts`. The floor dot is the calmest point near the median colour of the 0.72–0.95 band, and nothing requires it to sit on the floor. In the living room it lands on the sofa, and in the bedroom on the bedspread. From there Floor grows up to the 0.5 line.

Tolerances are loose: `global` is 18 for Walls and 22 for Floor, and `LW=0.5` halves lightness differences. A white wall therefore floods a white ceiling, the curtains, the worktops and the bedding.

The surfaces are grown independently and applied in order, so Floor paints over Walls. Nothing makes them exclusive.

- `engine/app/upload-bedroom-walls-floor-screen.png`: sage on the curtains, pillows and part of the bedspread; walnut on the lower back wall and the bed, with a hard seam across the photo.

1. **`lib/visualizer/model.ts` `fallbackDetection`: drop the `within` boxes.** They should only decide where seeds may sit, never clip the region. Keep them as metadata if anything needs them.

2. **`lib/visualizer/engine/segment.ts`: add a `GrowOpts.edgeStop?: number`.** Compute a Sobel magnitude on L* over the small copy, and refuse a step into a pixel whose gradient is above the threshold (about 12). Only the fallback passes it, so the samples' curated hulls are untouched. For the fallback surfaces, tighten `global` (Walls about 12, Floor about 16, Ceiling about 10) and weight lightness fully (`LW` 1 through an option), so a white wall stops at a white ceiling, curtain or bedding.

3. **`lib/visualizer/engine/fallback.ts`: pick the Floor seed from rows 0.88–0.98, with two conditions.** It must lie in a component connected to the bottom edge, and its colour must be more than ΔE 12 from the Walls seed. If nothing qualifies, return `floor: null` (make the type nullable), leave Floor unmarked and let the studio add it through the existing "add it by name and tap where it is" or Draw a surface.

4. **Make the fallback surfaces exclusive** in `lib/visualizer/engine/run.ts`, after the masks are grown and only for `detection.source === 'fallback'`. Where two masks overlap, give the pixel to the surface whose seed Lab is nearest, and add a weak vertical prior: Floor loses above the Walls seed's y, and Ceiling loses below it.

verdict.reason:
The code shows it and the auditor's screenshots show it. In growRegion, the hull and cutout polygons become 0/1 `blocked` cells on the downscaled copy (480 px long side, or 640 on High quality). The closed mask is then zeroed on those cells, and `upscaleMask` scales it up bilinearly and applies smoothstep((v-0.3)/0.4). That narrow smoothstep turns the 3x-plus upscaled cell edge into a nearly hard step, so a shallow curated line (the ceiling/wall line 0.322,0.25 → 1,0.162, floor hull edges, wall bases, worktops) turns into a staircase. Each step is a few screen pixels tall.

zf-ceiling-before.png shows regular flat runs about 0.05 wide with a jump between each. app/z-v4-right.png shows the same on the navy wall's ceiling line and on the floor/wall base by the plant. zf-ceiling.png (the prototype of the fix) gives a clean anti-aliased line along the same edge.

Adjacent sample surfaces share hull edges, for example the living room's ceiling and back wall. So each side of the shared line steps on its own and the seam reads as jagged. In the demo the sample rooms are the showcase, so a studio would notice.

Severity: major is fair for a pitch prototype whose selling point is the render, though it is cosmetic rather than functional.

A separate, related artefact, not part of this finding: the `exclude` boxes still cut hard rectangles, for example the rectangle behind the plant pot in z-v4-right.png. Those are axis-aligned, so they do not staircase.
verdict.fix:
Only lib/visualizer/engine/segment.ts changes; callers in lib/visualizer/engine/run.ts stay as they are.

1. In growRegion, keep two copies of the polygons. The first is `hull`/`cutout` in small-copy coordinates, used only for `blocked`, with the hull grown outwards by about 2 cells (offset each vertex from the centroid by 2/w and 2/h in 0…1 space, or dilate the hull-blocked complement by 2 before marking). The cutouts are shrunk by about 1 cell the same way, so the flood reaches the true line instead of stopping one cell short.
2. After `upscaleMask`, both in the `key` branch and the flood branch, build a full-resolution clip:
   - hullClip = the maximum of `polygonMask(img.width, img.height, p)` over `o.hull` (the 0…1 points, not the scaled ones), clamped to 1.
   - cutClip = the maximum of `polygonMask(...)` over `o.cutout`.
   - Then `out[i] *= hullClip[i] * (1 - cutClip[i])`.
3. Use a single helper, `clipToOutlines(mask, W, H, hull, cutout)`, called in both return paths.

`polygonMask` already supersamples 4 times per row, so shared hull edges between neighbouring surfaces get complementary coverage and the seam comes out clean.

Cost: one polygonMask per polygon at full size, run once per region computation. Regions are already computed once per surface in run.ts, so no new cache is needed unless profiling says otherwise.

Leave `within` and `exclude` boxes as cell blocks; they are axis-aligned and do not staircase.

Verify with a before/after crop of the living room ceiling line, the floor base and the kitchen worktop at 100 % on :3011, per CLAUDE.md's recipe, and log a bug-fix REG entry.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this by reading the code. I didn't re-render it. In lib/visualizer/materials.ts:13, `fromCatalogue` always sets `imageUrl: null`, and `pattern` comes only from `WALLPAPER_PATTERNS` (`patternOf` in patterns.ts:25). So a catalogue flooring, tile or stone material carries only a hex colour.

In engine/run.ts:92-96, `textureFor` returns a texture only for a pattern or for `category === 'Wallpapers' && imageUrl`. That means a studio or design material with a photo in Flooring, Tiles or Stone, such as sm-walnut-vinyl, paints its hex even though its picker chip (`chipCss`) shows the photo. `refinish` (run.ts:100) likewise lays only patterns and never uses `imageUrl`.

In engine/recolor.ts:32-36, the shading is `L = Lt * shade`, with `shade` = the photo's L divided by the region mean, clamped to 0.2–1.6. That full-resolution ratio carries the old surface's grout lines and grain straight onto the new material. The multiplication then pushes a light material (Lt around 90) past 100 wherever shade > ~1.1, and `Math.min(100, …)` clips it flat, which is why the sunlit patches and the subway wall go white. Gloss adds further toward 100 on top of that.

So the mean colour is right, but there's no material structure and the old structure prints through. That matches the auditor's evidence. On floors and backsplashes, where studios judge the render, it is a real major issue.
verdict.fix:
1) engine/recolor.ts: split the photo's lightness into light and detail. Light is a box-blurred L* (r ≈ W/100, about 5–6 px at 480–640) divided by the region mean, clamped as today. Detail is L − blur(L). Rebuild as L = base·light + detailGain·detail. Use detailGain ≈ 1 when the new material's category matches what the surface reads as (a paint → paint recolour), and ≈ 0.25 when it differs (tile → wood, wood → tile) or when a texture is supplied. That way old grout and boards don't print.

Above light = 1, replace the linear multiply with a shoulder, L = Lt + (100 − Lt)·(1 − exp(−(light − 1)·k)) with k ≈ 2, so light materials keep a gradient in the sun. The gloss and satin highlight then adds on top of that without hard clipping.

2) patterns.ts: add procedural tiles next to the wallpapers, keyed by catalogue subcategory rather than by id, and extend `patternOf` to take the CatalogueItem, or add a `surfacePatternOf(c)`. The kinds are: plank (grain streaks + staggered joints) for Hardwood / Engineered / Vinyl / Bamboo / Laminate; herringbone and chevron; grid tile with grout for Subway (2:1 offset) / Large Format / Square, plus hex; and marble / quartz veining (low-frequency noise veins). Each also needs a `patternCss` so the chip matches the render.

3) engine/run.ts `textureFor` and `refinish`: use `m.imageUrl` as the tile for Flooring, Laminates, Tiles, Stone and Countertops, not only Wallpapers, and route `refinish` through the same `textureFor`. Scale the tile by category: about 1/8 of the width for floor planks and tiles, 1/20 for subway tile.

Treat laying floor tiles through a homography from a quad hull as a follow-up, shared with the wallpaper perspective finding. Without it, the tiles lie flat in screen space, which is still far better than a flat colour.

Verify with the auditor's repro on :3011 (Oak Herringbone on the living room, Walnut Engineered on the kitchen, Subway Tile White on the walls). Check that the near-white fraction on the subway wall falls back near the original, and bank the shots under design-source/verify/ai-visualizer/. Log it as a bug-fix REG entry.

kept.title: Relight presets don't deliver what their cards show: Daylight burns out, Blue Hour and Spotlight barely change, night presets keep a daylit window, lights glow in the wrong places
kept.where: Editor › Lighting, all six presets, all three rooms, 1440
kept.evidence: In the app from the Original: Blue Hour, Directional Spotlight, Daylight and Warm Cozy Home (<E>/sheet-app-misc.jpg rows 1–2; files <E>/app/light-*.jpg). In Node, all six presets on all rooms (<E>/sheet-light-lr.jpg, <E>/sheet-light-kt.jpg). Daylight clips 18.2 % (living) and 32.5 % (kitchen) of the photo to white, against 0.2–0.3 % in the originals: the kitchen island's waterfall merges into the floor (<E>/z-kt-day.png). Blue Hour and Overcast are hard to tell from the original, and Spotlight is only a warm dim with no pools of light. The cards' previews (public/visualizer/lighting/*.jpg, <E>/sheet-light-previews.jpg) promise a deep blue dusk and dark rooms with lit lamps. Warm Cozy and Blue Hour keep the garden window fully daylit. Pendants 'on' in Warm Cozy leave the kitchen's three pendants unlit (<E>/z-kt-cozy.png), because grade.ts glows sit at fixed spots (pendants x 0.36/0.5/0.64, y 0.3) and not at the room's pendant lights (0.552/0.657/0.746, y ≈ 0.27).
kept.repro: Any sample → Lighting › each preset → Generate; compare with the card image.
kept.fix: engine/grade.ts: 1) Grade in linear light with a filmic shoulder instead of `r*bright` then clamp; Daylight's intensity 80 gives a gain of 1.27, so compress highlights (for example Reinhard on luminance) so less than 2 % of pixels clip. 2) Night and dusk (sunAngle ≤ 10 or 0): cut exposure further (×0.45 blue hour, ×0.35 warm cozy). Add a `windows` polygon to each SampleRoom in samples.ts and darken and cool it (a night sky) instead of keeping daylight. 3) Take the glow centres from the reading: pieces in category 'Lighting' (kitchen pendants, the bedroom lamp, the living-room floor lamp at 0.32,0.48), plus downlight positions per sample. Add them in linear space with a hot core under each shade, and pass them into grade from runPass. 4) Spotlight: a 0.5 exposure base plus the fixtures, not the mild −24 intensity it is now.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this from the code and the auditor's renders. I didn't need to change the server.

1) **Daylight burns out.** `grade.ts` scales each channel by `bright = 0.55 + intensity/100·0.9` and then clamps. For Daylight (intensity 80) that gain is 1.27, so every channel above about 0.79 goes to white. The kitchen sheet shows it: the island's waterfall, the worktops and the floor merge into white.

2) **Night presets keep the daylit window.** Night is a flat multiply of about 0.84 (`night = 0.18`, or `dusk = 0.16`), with a soft-light tint on top and no mask for the windows. So Blue Hour, Warm Cozy and Spotlight come out as mild tints of the daylit photo. The garden window stays bright. None of them reaches the dark rooms with lit lamps that the preset previews in `public/visualizer/lighting/*.jpg` show. Spotlight (intensity 26) only gets a 0.78 gain and a warm tint, with no pools of light.

3) **Glows sit in the wrong places.** `glows()` puts pendants at fixed x 0.36/0.5/0.64, y 0.3, and downlights at fixed spots. The kitchen sample's pendants are Lighting pieces at 0.552/0.657/0.746, y ≈ 0.27 (`samples.ts` lines 98–100). In `z-kt-cozy.png` all three shades are unlit while an empty ceiling area glows.

The shortcut to 1.0's finished image in `relightPass` only exists for the bedroom's Golden Hour (`samples.ts:61`). Every other preset and room goes through this grade.

Refuting points: none apply. There is no image model, but that doesn't excuse clipped highlights or glows away from the fixtures. The sample already knows where its lamps are.
verdict.fix:
These are all engine fixes, with no UI change.

1) **`lib/visualizer/engine/grade.ts`: grade in linear light.**
   - Convert sRGB to linear, apply the exposure gain, then compress with a luminance shoulder (Reinhard-style, `L' = L·(1 + L/Lw²)/(1 + L)` scaling rgb by `L'/L`), then convert back to sRGB.
   - Target under 2% clipped pixels for Daylight on all three samples. Add a check for that to the probe.

2) **Night and dusk (`sunAngle` 0, or ≤ 10 with a cool temperature).**
   - Cut exposure much harder than the current ×0.84: about ×0.45 for dusk and ×0.35 for night.
   - Add an optional `windows` hull list to `SampleRoom` in `lib/visualizer/samples.ts`, in the same shape as the existing surface hulls: the living room's full-height glazing and far window, the kitchen's garden window, the bedroom window.
   - In grade, pull those windows toward a deep blue night sky instead of leaving them daylit. Pass them as a new optional `grade(img, knobs, amount, scene?)` argument.
   - Photos that aren't samples keep today's behaviour.

3) **Glows at the room's own fixtures.**
   - Build the glow list from the sample's pieces with `category === 'Lighting'`: the kitchen's three pendants, the bedroom's table lamp, and a new living-room floor-lamp piece.
   - Add `downlights` / `cove` points per sample in `samples.ts`. Keep the fixed positions only as the fallback for photos that aren't samples.
   - Add the glow in linear space with a hot core just under each shade's box plus a wide warm falloff.
   - Thread the scene from `relightPass`, `editPass` (the `light` / `extra.preset` path) and `previewLight` in `lib/visualizer/engine/run.ts`.

4) **Spotlight.** Give it an exposure base of about 0.5, plus pools under the downlights and accent points. The fixtures should make the look, not the current mild intensity-26 dim.

`lib/visualizer/lighting.ts` needs no change beyond optionally re-tuning the knobs once the grade responds properly. Log the change as a bug fix in `design-source/REGISTER.md`. Verify with a Node sheet of the six presets × three rooms next to the preview cards, plus the clip-percentage gate.

kept.title: Style transfer from a mood board paints the walls the board's paper and the floor its darkest swatch, not the walnut the board names
kept.where: Editor › Style › Or borrow a look from a photo, Living room, 1440
kept.evidence: In the app I uploaded public/uat-files/kitchen-moodboard.jpg (Calacatta, walnut laminate, navy cabinets, brass, grey tile, sage) as the reference on the Original and Generated (<E>/app/transfer-moodboard.jpg, panel <E>/app/transfer-panel.png). The walls turned the board's white paper background, the floor turned dark slate (the navy-cabinet swatch) with the same rug-rectangle seam, and the rug was whitened as a rectangle including the floor corners. transferPass sorts the palette by lightness and maps lightest → walls, darkest → floor, and extractPalette counts the board's background as a colour.
kept.repro: Living room → Original → Style → Upload a reference → kitchen-moodboard.jpg → Generate.
kept.fix: engine/run.ts transferPass and engine/palette.ts: 1) Drop a dominant flat near-white or near-grey colour covering over 35 % of the reference with low local variance: it is the page, not a material. 2) Map by role, not by lightness. Floor takes the palette colour nearest a wood hue (Lab hue 40–80°, L 25–65), else the darkest neutral. Walls take the lightest non-background neutral. Cabinets and joinery take the most saturated dark colour. Countertops and backsplash take the lightest. 3) Soft furniture (the rug) should use the traced cuts from the Customize finding.

verdict.reason:
The code confirms the mechanism. `transferPass` (lib/visualizer/engine/run.ts:263-277) sorts the reference colours by luminance only. Walls/ceiling take `pal[0]` (lightest), Floor takes `pal[pal.length-1]` (darkest), cabinets take `pal[2]`, and countertops/backsplash take `pal[0]`. `extractPalette` (palette.ts) runs k=5 k-means over the whole 64 px image. It has no background handling, so the board's off-white paper (about 45% of kitchen-moodboard.jpg) merges with the Calacatta swatch into the lightest cluster. With six swatches plus the paper squeezed into five clusters, the walnut never becomes the darkest centre and cannot reach the floor.

The auditor's render (scratchpad/audit/engine/app/transfer-moodboard.jpg) shows this. The floor came out a cold green-grey, the navy and sage mix, not walnut. The rug was left as a raw rectangle with an untouched floor corner at the lower right, which leaves a visible seam.

Two details are off. The walls "turning the paper" is barely visible, because the sample's walls were already near-white and a paper-white wall is a defensible pick. And the floor is navy/sage grey, not strictly "dark slate". The real, felt defect is role-blind mapping: a board that labels "Walnut laminate" gives a grey-green floor. That is exactly the demo moment the mood-board step (UAT) exercises, so major stands. The rug-rectangle seam is a separate segmentation issue (the Customize/traced-cut finding), not part of this palette fix.
verdict.fix:
1) lib/visualizer/engine/palette.ts: add an optional `dropPage` step to `extractPalette`, and have the transfer path use it. Sample the image's border pixels (the outer 4 px of the 64 px copy). A cluster that owns more than 60% of the border and more than 30% of the pixels is the page, so leave it out of the returned palette. Also raise k to 6-7 when the page is dropped, so each swatch keeps its own cluster. Plain photos keep today's behaviour (no cluster dominates the border), and the palette chips shown in Applied lose the paper too.

2) lib/visualizer/engine/run.ts `transferPass`: replace the luminance-index picks with role picks over the deduped palette, using a small Lab/HSL helper (reuse `pixels.ts` conversions if present):
- Floor = the colour nearest a wood hue (hue 20-45°, sat 0.2-0.6, L 25-65), else the darkest low-saturation neutral.
- Walls/Ceiling/Trim = the lightest remaining neutral (sat < 0.15).
- Feature walls/Panelling = the most saturated mid-tone.
- Cabinets/Wardrobes/Doors/Open shelving = the most saturated dark colour, else the darkest.
- Countertops/Backsplash = the lightest.
- Soft furniture = the most saturated mid-tone not already used.

Variants 2 and 3 should rotate within each role's candidates (next-nearest) instead of rotating the whole light-sorted list. Keep `a.palette` as the page-free palette.

3) Leave the rug-rectangle seam to the traced-cut fix in the Customize finding. Probe: Living room → Style → kitchen-moodboard.jpg → Generate. Assert that the floor's mean pixel sits near #8B6F55 and that no palette chip is paper-white.

kept.title: After a style transfer, the kept reference hijacks the next Generate: a typed note re-runs the transfer and the note is ignored
kept.where: Editor › Describe a change after any Style transfer version, 1440
kept.evidence: After the transfer above, I showed the Original, typed 'terracotta walls, walnut floor, warmer evening light' into Describe a change and pressed Generate. The new version is another 'Style transfer' identical to the previous one: white walls, slate floor (<E>/app/note-terracotta.jpg vs <E>/app/transfer-moodboard.jpg; screen <E>/app/note-terracotta-screen.png shows 'Your changes · Reference · 1' and the button 'Style transfer'). readNote parses the note correctly: {paints: wall Terracotta #C1694F, floor Walnut #6B4A2E, lighting warm-cozy} (<E>/note.mts). The note never runs because model.ts `afterRender` keeps `transfer.refs`, and `intentFor` returns 'transfer' before 'note' whenever refs exist.
kept.repro: Style → Upload a reference → Generate. Then type a note in Describe a change → Generate.
kept.fix: lib/visualizer/model.ts: in `afterRender`, clear `transfer.refs` like every other spent pick (keep strength, aspects and geometry as habits). Or, in `intentFor`, rank a typed note above leftover refs, and make the note pass ignore refs. Also show the note as a 'Note' chip in Your changes so the studio sees what Generate will apply.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this from the code; I didn't need a live run to see it. In lib/visualizer/model.ts:96, `afterRender` clears every spent pick but carries `transfer.refs` forward. In `intentFor` (model.ts:149-165), `refs` is checked on line 161, before `note` on line 164. So once a transfer has run, the leftover reference makes every later Generate another 'Style transfer', and the button label says so. The note is never passed to the transfer pass. `notePass` (engine/run.ts) handles only the 'note' intent, so a typed note is silently dropped.

The auditor's parsing claim is also consistent with the code: `readNote` would turn that sentence into wall and floor paints plus a lighting preset. I found nothing in the audit (16-…) or the register saying the reference should outlive its render. The comment on `afterRender` itself says "what it applied is spent", which the refs line contradicts.

One part of the suggested fix is already done. Your changes already shows a 'Your note' chip (visualizer-editor.tsx:292), next to 'Reference · n'. So the problem is not that the note is invisible. It's that the leftover reference wins, and after one transfer the studio has no reason to expect it's still set. Major is right: a studio's typed instruction produces a copy of the previous version with no explanation.
verdict.fix:
In lib/visualizer/model.ts, change `afterRender` so the spent references are dropped. Keep strength, aspects and geometry as habits, the same way quality and variants are kept:
`transfer: { ...emptyPending().transfer, strength: p.transfer.strength, aspects: p.transfer.aspects, geometry: p.transfer.geometry }` (no `refs`).

Leave `intentFor`'s order alone. A reference picked in the same round should still win over a note, which is 1.0's matrix. Once references are cleared after a render, the note wins naturally on the next round.

No new UI is needed. The 'Your note' chip already exists, and the Reference chip disappears when refs are cleared. If the studio wants the same reference on another version, the Style panel's reference well is one re-upload away. If keeping it is judged valuable, add a small 'Use again' action on that well rather than a hidden carry-over.

Then re-run the transfer → note repro in the visualizer probe (design-source/verify/ai-visualizer/) and check that the second version's kind is 'note' with terracotta walls and a walnut floor.

kept.title: Wallpaper is laid flat in screen space: no perspective on receding walls, a fixed scale, printed across shelves, and 40 % flatter than the wall's light
kept.where: Editor › Walls › Wallpapers, Living room and Kitchen, 1440
kept.evidence: Vertical Stripe Navy on the kitchen's right wall, which recedes sharply (its ceiling line falls from y 0.2 to 0.12): the stripes stay equal-width and vertical in image space, run over the floating shelf boards (0.85–0.93, 0.345), and leave pale boxes around the shelf objects (<E>/z-kt-wallR.png). On the living-room wall the stripes look pasted on. The white stripes are near-flat because `soften` is worked out from the base hex (navy) and applied to the accent too (<E>/z-lr-stripe.png). The tile is always width/20 px (engine/run.ts textureFor), whatever the wall's size or distance.
kept.repro: Kitchen → Walls → Vertical Stripe Navy → Generate; Living room → Walls → Tropical Botanical.
kept.fix: engine/recolor.ts `recolor(texture)`: 1) When the surface's hull is a quad (the curated walls are), compute the homography from the hull to a unit rectangle, sample the tile at (u·wallWidthTiles, v·wallHeightTiles), and scale by the wall's real size (for example 0.53 m roll width, assuming 2.7 m ceilings). 2) Work out `soften` per texel from the texel's own L, not the base hex's. 3) Add the shelves as wall cutouts in samples.ts.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this in the code and in the auditor's zoomed shots. I did not re-run it on :3016, because the code is enough to decide it.

- **Tiled in screen space.** `recolor()` reads the tile at `tex[(y % texture.height) * texture.width + (x % texture.width)]` (lib/visualizer/engine/recolor.ts:35), so the pattern lines up with the picture's pixels, not the wall.
- **Same size everywhere.** The tile is always `Math.max(18, round(width/20))` (run.ts:93, and the same at run.ts:101). Every wall, near or far, gets the same stripe width.
- **Stripes look flat.** `soften` is worked out once from the gap between the base hex (navy) and the patch's mean light (recolor.ts:26-27). It is then applied to the tile's own L as well. A dark base on a white wall gives a large gap, `soften` reaches its cap, and the shading is pressed toward flat, which is worst on the light stripes.
- **Shots match.** z-kt-wallR.png shows equal-width vertical stripes on the kitchen's receding right wall. They run straight across both floating shelf boards (about y 0.345 and 0.40), and rectangles of the old white wall show around the shelf objects. Those rectangles are the surface's `exclude` boxes, and there is no cutout for the boards. z-lr-stripe.png shows the living-room wall's stripes stuck flat on the wall, with no perspective and almost no shading.

On the three sample rooms a studio would see this as "pasted on" in a demo. Minor fits: the finish still reads, and paint colours are not affected.
verdict.fix:
1. **lib/visualizer/engine/recolor.ts**
   - Add an optional `frame` to `recolor`: the surface's quad hull in pixels, plus the number of repeats across its width and height.
   - When a frame is given, work out the 3×3 homography from the unit square to the quad once. Per pixel, invert it to get (u, v) and sample the tile at `(u*repeatsX mod 1, v*repeatsY mod 1)`, with bilinear sampling rather than nearest.
   - Without a frame (hulls that aren't quads, or non-sample photos), keep today's screen-space tiling.
   - Change `soften` for textures: compute the gap per texel from the texel's own L (T[0]) against `mean`, not from `Lt`, so the light stripes keep the wall's light. A simpler option is to cap `soften` at about 0.35 when a texture is present.
2. **lib/visualizer/engine/run.ts**
   - `textureFor` and the refinish path (lines 92-101): build a fixed-resolution tile (for example 64 px) and pass the frame instead of `width/20`.
   - Set repeatsY from the surface's height, for example 2.7 m divided by the pattern's repeat. Set repeatsX from the quad's aspect, using the average of the near and far edge lengths. That way the same pattern has the same real size on every wall.
3. **lib/visualizer/samples.ts**
   - Mark each curated wall's single 4-point `hull` as the quad to use.
   - On the kitchen's right wall, add `cutout` polygons for the two floating shelf boards and the objects on them. Tighten or replace the rectangular `exclude` boxes there with polygons so no pale boxes are left behind. Do the same for the living-room wall's frame, TV and vase if their boxes show.
4. **Verify** with a probe on Kitchen → Vertical Stripe Navy and on Living room → Tropical Botanical. Check that the stripes narrow toward the far end of the kitchen's right wall, that the boards stay in front of the stripes, and that the light stripes keep the wall's shading. Bank the shots under design-source/verify/ai-visualizer/.

This changes no UI and needs no new copy.

kept.title: Restyle on a sample room drops the version's edits: restyling V2 returns the same stock render as restyling the Original
kept.where: Editor › Style › a style card, from any edited version of a sample room
kept.evidence: From V2 (sage walls, walnut floor, emerald sofa) → Style › Industrial → Generate returned /visualizer/samples/living-room/industrial.jpg unchanged: 1.0's finished render, with none of V2's picks (<E>/app/restyle-industrial-from-v2.jpg; log line 'src /visualizer/samples/living-room/industrial.jpg'). restylePass ignores i.base when `sample.looks[style]` exists. kept.repro: Living room → V2 → Style › Industrial → Generate.

verdict.reason:

It also resets the finishes to surfaces {}, removed [], customized {}, reshaped true. kept.title: A faint light stepped line where two painted surfaces meet
kept.where: Editor, walls and ceiling painted in the same pass, Living room
kept.evidence: The back wall, the wall above the window and the ceiling all in Navy leave a light stepped line along the wall and ceiling junction (0.55–0.85, 0.17–0.21) (<E>/z-seam.png). Each mask is about 0.5 on the shared edge, and the sequential `recolor` blends leave about 25 % of the original white.
kept.repro: Surfaces › Walls + Ceiling → Navy Accent → Generate → zoom on the ceiling line.
kept.fix: In editPass, gather each pixel's target colour and weight across all surfaces in the pass and composite once: alpha = min(1, Σw), colour = Σ(w·C)/Σw. Together with the full-res polygon clip (the staircase finding), shared edges then sum to 1.

verdict.reason:
The finding is real, but you only see it when zoomed in. Painted surfaces with a drawn outline get their mask from `polygonMask` (lib/visualizer/engine/segment.ts:124). That mask is anti-aliased with 4 sub-rows, so two outlines that share an edge each give a boundary pixel about half coverage, and the two halves add up to 1.

In `editPass` (run.ts, the `p.materials` loop), `restylePass` and `refinish`, each surface is painted onto the image one after another with `recolor`. Each call blends in place: d += (C - d)·m. Two blends of about 0.5 therefore reach only 1 - (1 - a)(1 - b) ≈ 0.75, and about 25% of the original pixel is left.

It gets slightly worse. The second `recolor` works out its light from the pixel the first one already changed, compared with its own surface's average. So the seam pixel is neither the original colour nor a clean Navy.

The auditor's zoomed image (audit/engine/z-seam.png) shows exactly this. A thin, lighter stepped line runs along the join between the wall and the ceiling, from about x 0.55 to 0.85 and y 0.17 to 0.21, on an otherwise even Navy. At 1× it is a hairline, and only a dark paint over a white original shows it. So this stays polish, not major.

The steps in the line come from the outline's own coverage and resolution (the separate staircase finding). The light gap is caused by the one-after-another compositing alone.
verdict.fix:
In lib/visualizer/engine/recolor.ts, split `recolor` in two without changing its maths.
- `shadeTarget(img, mask, hex, sheen, strength, texture, acc)` keeps the existing shading code (light ratio from the region's average, soften, gloss/satin, grain, texture tile). It reads the untouched pixel and adds into an accumulator `{ r, g, b, w: Float32Array }` instead of writing to the image: `acc.w[i] += m`, and `acc.r[i] += m * nr`, likewise for g and b.
- `composite(img, acc)` then writes each pixel once: `a = min(1, w)`, `C = acc / w`, `d += (C - d) * a`.
- `recolor` stays as a wrapper around the two, so every single-surface caller behaves exactly as it does today.

In lib/visualizer/engine/run.ts, use one accumulator per variant wherever several surfaces are painted in the same pass:
- `editPass`: the `p.materials` loop and the note-paints surfaces loop
- `restylePass`: the per-surface loop
- `refinish`: line 101

Call `composite` once after each loop. Leave furniture recolours and plate pastes sequential. They sit on top of surfaces by design, and a piece does not share an edge with a wall's outline.

Because every surface's light is now read from the original pixels, the seam pixel gets the same light as its neighbours. Where the outlines' coverage adds up to 1, the seam lands at exactly the new colour.

Check it with a probe on the Living room sample (Walls + Ceiling → Navy Accent → Generate). Sample the pixels along the join (0.55–0.85, 0.17–0.21) and confirm they come within about 3 in lightness of the Navy on either side. Also confirm that a single-surface edit is byte-identical to the current output.
